passage: At dinner time in their city flat, Akash sat over his laptop with a deadline. To keep Aparna quiet, he handed her the phone with a cartoon. She watched, still and silent. Then she looked up and pointed at the window. "Papa, look, look!" A pigeon sat on the ledge. Akash, eyes on the screen, said "Mm-hm." She said it again. This time he shut the laptop, lifted her up to the glass and said, "Bird! A grey bird." She squealed and tapped the window.

qa.q: What was on the window ledge that Aparna pointed at?
qa.a: A pigeon was sitting on the window ledge.

qa.q: What was Aparna wanting when she said "Papa, look, look!"?
qa.a: She was probably excited by the pigeon and wanted her father to share the moment, since the cartoon gave her something to watch but not a person.

qa.q: What could Akash do about the phone and his daily time with Aparna?
qa.a: Use the phone as a tool now and then, not a babysitter, and make time each day to talk and play with her.

qa.q: How might Akash have felt when he first said "Mm-hm" and later when he shut the laptop?
qa.a: He was probably stressed by the deadline at first, and perhaps a little guilty and glad when he noticed how much the pigeon mattered to her.

grounding: Shows a toddler handed a phone to keep quiet who gets stimulation but no person until her father looks up and joins her.

passage:
On the Mumbai local, Baljeet handed Nilesh, two, a phone full of cartoons to keep him quiet. Nilesh stared, silent.

At home, Baljeet sat on the sofa with his own phone. Nilesh held up a toy. No one looked.

That night Baljeet noticed Nilesh knew no new words. The next evening he left the phone aside and they named every car from the balcony. Nilesh chattered.

qa.q: What did Baljeet and Nilesh name from the balcony?
qa.a: They named every car from the balcony.

qa.q: What might Nilesh have been feeling when no one looked at his toy?
qa.a: Nilesh probably felt lonely and ignored, wanting a person to share with.

qa.q: What did Baljeet change, and why does it matter?
qa.a: He put the phone aside and talked and played with Nilesh, treating the screen as a tool, not a babysitter.

qa.q: What might Baljeet have felt on noticing Nilesh knew no new words?
qa.a: Baljeet probably felt worried and a little guilty, realising the phone had replaced time together.

grounding: Shows a toddler given a phone instead of a person and a parent who begins talking and playing daily.

passage:
"Mumma, see!" Dilnaz, two, held up a leaf.

Deepika, typing, handed her the tablet. "Watch this, baby. Mumma's busy."

Dilnaz watched, silent, for an hour.

At bedtime, Dilnaz asked, "Mumma, play?"

Deepika paused. "Tomorrow, first thing, we'll play. No tablet."

Next morning they collected leaves in the park. Dilnaz talked the whole way.

qa.q: What did Dilnaz hold up to show her mother?
Why did Dilnaz ask "Mumma, play?" at bedtime?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt lonely and wanted her mother's company, not just the tablet.

qa.q: What did Deepika do that helped?
qa.a: She made time the next morning to play with Dilnaz without the tablet, treating it as a tool, not a babysitter.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel when Dilnaz asks to play?
qa.a: Deepika may feel a pang of guilt and realise Dilnaz needs her, not the screen.

grounding: Shows a toddler handed a tablet instead of attention and a parent who chooses daily play and talk.
